tldr: By using a quasi-direct drive (QDD) with an 18:1 gear ratio, researchers developed an active knee prosthesis that matches or beats commercial products in weight (2.6 kg) and build height (24.5 cm), while delivering a biological-level peak torque of 145 Nm.
hero_caption: Appearance of the developed QDD knee prosthesis (left), along with torque-speed boundaries at an 18:1 gear ratio and thermal analysis results during stair climbing (right). It achieves a compact packaging viable for practical use as a full leg prosthesis including the foot, while covering output capabilities needed for everyday tasks.
overview:
Traditional passive or microprocessor-controlled knee prostheses work well enough for level-ground walking. However, they cannot generate positive work on their own, such as pushing the joint powerfully during stair ascent or sit-to-stand transitions. As a result, users are forced to rely on compensatory movements that overload their intact limb and lower back, often leading to chronic back pain and osteoarthritis. Powered prostheses with built-in motors have been studied to address this. Yet, obtaining sufficient torque usually requires high gear ratios (e.g., over 100:1). This creates clear trade-offs: the joints become mechanically stiff, generate loud acoustic noise, and lose backdrivability (the ability to yield smoothly to external forces).

Quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuation—combining a high-torque motor with a small gear ratio—has gained strong interest as an alternative. While QDD is well known in quadruped robots for its high responsiveness and backdrivability, applying it to prostheses has historically led to oversized motors that are simply too heavy and tall for practical adoption.

In this paper, the authors conducted multi-objective optimization of an 18:1 two-stage transmission combined with thermal and structural finite element analysis (FEA). By using the outer frame itself as a heat sink, they achieved a total weight of about 2.6 kg (including battery) and a build height of 24.5 cm. This matches or improves upon a leading commercial powered knee (Össur Power Knee). Benchtop tests demonstrated a backdrive torque below 1 Nm, a peak torque of 145 Nm, and high-precision torque control. Furthermore, walking and sit-to-stand trials with three individuals with transfemoral amputation confirmed biological-level joint torques and kinematics, alongside significantly quieter operation compared to the commercial device.
contributions: Optimized an 18:1 two-stage transmission using thermal and structural analysis alongside a multi-objective genetic algorithm, creating a QDD knee prosthesis weighing 2.6 kg (including battery)—lighter than a commercial unit (2.7 kg).
Simultaneously achieved an extremely low backdrive torque of ~0.98 Nm without external torque sensors, a biomimetic peak torque of 145 Nm, and high-bandwidth open-loop torque tracking.

Demonstrated biomimetic joint torques and kinematics during level-ground walking and sit-to-stand transitions with three individuals with transfemoral amputation across different mobility levels (K3 and K4).
Reduced build height by 6.3 cm, increased peak torque by ~81%, and lowered acoustic noise by an average of 3.9 dB (and ~4.8 dB peak) compared to a commercial powered knee (Össur Power Knee).

sections.heading: The Powered Prosthesis Dilemma: Breaking the Power-Weight Trade-off
sections.summary: Because conventional knee prostheses cannot perform positive work, amputees must rely on compensatory movements. Powered prostheses help, but have suffered from heavy weight, high gear ratio noise, and joint stiffness. QDD offers superior backdrivability and control, but past prototypes were too bulky. This work tackles that challenge by building a compact, lightweight QDD knee that outperforms commercial devices.
sections.details:
Many individuals with lower-limb amputations rely on compensatory behaviors using their intact limb during daily activities. This often triggers osteoarthritis and chronic lower back pain. Powered knee prostheses can perform positive work by generating torque autonomously, significantly relieving these burdens.

However, enabling a 100 kg user to climb stairs or stand up requires massive peak knee torques of 120 to 145 Nm. Traditional powered knees achieved this by pairing small motors with large reduction ratios, such as belts, harmonic drives, or series elastic actuators (SEAs). This approach introduces distinct drawbacks:
- Drivetrain inertia and friction increase, making the joint mechanically rigid and incapable of compliant reaction to external forces (lack of backdrivability).
- High-frequency, uncomfortable acoustic noise is generated.
- Impedance and torque control become complex and bandwidth-limited.

Quasi-direct drive (QDD) addresses these issues by keeping gear ratios low. QDD offers transparency (low output impedance) close to direct-drive motors, allowing accurate torque control using motor current alone. However, prior QDD knee prototypes weighed around 3.5 kg for the knee alone (6.5 kg with the foot), had shifted centers of rotation (CoR), and were too tall to fit shorter users—presenting fatal hurdles for clinical translation.

Through rigorous structural and thermal design optimization, this work achieved a mass of 2.60 kg and a build height of 24.5 cm, outperforming a leading commercial powered knee (Össur Power Knee: 2.70 kg, 30.8 cm build height). The goal is to prove the clinical viability of QDD prostheses for the first time.

sections.heading: Lean Mechanical Design Carved Out by Thermal Analysis and Genetic Algorithms
sections.summary: Based on design specs for a 102 kg user, the team developed a custom BLDC motor that uses the frame as a heat sink, paired with an optimized 18:1 two-stage transmission. Detailed structural, thermal, and dimensional analyses yielded a lightweight, low-profile package.
sections.details:
### Setting Design Requirements
Requirements were established based on kinematic and kinetic data from a 102 kg user (75th percentile adult male). To preserve biomimetic impedance, reflected rotor inertia (which scales with the square of the gear ratio) was constrained to be below 10% of biological shank-foot pendulum inertia ($0.038\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$).

### Motor Selection and Thermal Design
A custom CubeMars frameless BLDC motor (RI8523) was selected, featuring a measured torque constant of 0.175 Nm/A. Achieving a 145 Nm peak torque with an 18:1 gear ratio requires the motor to repeatedly deliver ~8.06 Nm, slightly exceeding its continuous rating (7.8 Nm). Because this is a thermal bottleneck, the motor windings were potted directly to the aluminum alloy (7075-T6) chassis using thermally conductive epoxy, turning the entire frame into a heat sink. As a result, in a 600-step continuous stair ascent simulation, the frame surface temperature stabilized at 44.5°C—safely below the 48°C touch limit.

### Multi-Objective Optimization of the Two-Stage Transmission
The transmission uses a stepped-planet compound planetary gear train (SPC-PGT, 9:1) for the compact, high-ratio first stage, followed by a spur gear stage (2:1) that raises the center of rotation toward the body. Using design variables like module, tooth counts, and face widths, the team ran a multi-objective genetic algorithm. It minimized transmission mass and knee output gear radius while satisfying root bending stress limits (safety factor $\ge 1.25$) and the 18:1 total ratio. Hardened 420 stainless steel was selected for its high yield strength, allowing aggressive pocketing and weight reduction.

### Electronics and Architecture
A Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 (CM5) serves as the primary controller, linked to the motor driver (Elmo Twitter) via CAN bus to minimize wiring. The distal end houses a 6-axis load cell, alongside an IMU tracking thigh tilt. Outer cosmetic covers are held in place by neodymium magnets, allowing easy access for internal maintenance.

captions.P4: Exploded view of the two-stage transmission and transparent CAD rendering of the prosthesis interior. Combining the first-stage stepped-planet compound planetary gear train (SPC-PGT) with the second-stage spur gear pair compactly optimizes the center of rotation while substantially reducing overall build height.

sections.heading: From Benchtop Tests to User Walking: Verified Transparency and Biomechanics
sections.summary: Benchtop testing confirmed a low 0.98 Nm backdrive torque, 145 Nm peak torque, and accurate torque tracking. Trials with three individuals with transfemoral amputation during level walking and sit-to-stand tasks demonstrated biological joint torques, along with quieter performance than a commercial benchmark.
sections.details:
### Benchtop Tests: Superior QDD Transparency
- **Backdrive Torque**: The static torque required to manually backdrive the joint output was only 0.98 Nm. This indicates minimal cogging or friction, allowing the joint to yield smoothly to external forces.
- **Position and Torque Tracking**: Position step response rise times were 35–54 ms. Torque step responses (20 Nm, 40 Nm) were exceptionally fast, with rise times of 10.2–17.4 ms. Open-loop torque tracking errors on biological walking and stair profiles stayed within one-third of natural biological standard deviations.
- **Peak Torque**: While holding angle under position control, external loads were applied to confirm the actuator reliably holds the targeted 145 Nm output.

### Walking and Sit-to-Stand Trials with Amputee Participants
Three individuals with transfemoral amputation across varying mobility levels (two K4, one K3) tested the prosthesis during treadmill walking (0.8, 1.0, 1.2 m/s) and repeated sit-to-stand transitions (10 reps). Control was handled by a previously developed Hybrid Kinematic-Impedance Controller (HKIC).
- **Level-Ground Walking**: Across all speeds, knee angles and extension torques closely matched able-bodied reference data (within $\pm 1$ standard deviation). While a phase advance appeared due to the amputee-typical shortened stance phase, biomimetic trends—like increased peak swing flexion at higher speeds—were successfully reproduced.
- **Sit-to-Stand Transitions**: During sitting down, the device generated extension torque comparable to able-bodied references. Rising torque was slightly lower, likely due to testing with a passive prosthetic foot.

### Acoustic Noise Measurements
Acoustic noise during walking was recorded at a 1.5 m distance using a sound level meter. The QDD knee averaged 48.54 dB (peak 51.65 dB). Compared to the commercial Össur Power Knee running the same control algorithm (average 52.33 dB, peak 57.17 dB), the QDD knee was quieter by ~3.9 dB on average and ~4.8 dB at peak. Because decibels are logarithmic, this represents a noticeable reduction in perceived noise.

captions.P6: Benchtop validation results: torque step responses (left), torque tracking for stair climbing and walking (center), and manual peak loading test reaching 145 Nm (right). All tests show high responsiveness and close tracking of commanded values.
captions.P7: Experimental setup showing a participant with transfemoral amputation wearing the developed QDD knee prosthesis during level-ground treadmill walking (left) and sit-to-stand transitions (right).
captions.P8: Knee joint angle (top) and torque (bottom) profiles for three participants (P1–P3) across three walking speeds and sit-to-stand tasks. Participants demonstrated biomimetic patterns that closely align with the gray able-bodied reference bands (±1 SD).

sections.heading: Comparing with Commercial and Research Knees, Plus User Feedback
sections.summary: The knee is lighter, lower-profile, more powerful, and quieter than the commercial Power Knee, without suffering from torque drops near kinematic singularities like the Utah Knee. While users praised foot ground awareness, the study also revealed real-world needs like deeper knee flexion.
sections.details:
### Comparison with Prior Research and Commercial Devices
- **Comparison with Össur Power Knee**: The prototype is 100 g lighter and 6.3 cm shorter in build height. At the same time, peak torque increased by ~81% (from 80 Nm to 145 Nm), with lower acoustic noise.
- **Comparison with the Utah Knee (ball-screw hybrid drive, ~1.9 kg)**: While the Utah Knee is lighter, it suffers from a kinematic singularity at 88° of flexion where output torque drops sharply. Because this QDD design uses a fixed-ratio gear train, it delivers the full 145 Nm active torque across its entire 105° range of motion.

### User Feedback
Participants reported that early-to-mid stance ground feel (proprioception) was far clearer than with other powered or passive prostheses. This is a direct benefit of the low output impedance and mechanical transparency of QDD. Some also noted reduced physical effort and less lower back tightness while walking.

However, a K3 participant (P3) with weaker intact-limb strength provided a crucial insight. To rise from a chair, this user loaded the prosthetic side heavily, requiring about 120° of knee flexion—surpassing the able-bodied average (90–100°). The prototype hit its 105° mechanical hard stop. This highlighted that designs must account for compensatory motions in lower-mobility users rather than relying solely on able-bodied averages.

### Limitations and Next Steps
- **Continuous Run Time**: Because high-discharge LiPo batteries were chosen, estimated walking duration for a 102 kg user is roughly 2 hours (~8,300 steps). Commercial translation will require optimized battery cell packing and low-power embedded processors.
- **Sensor Weight Reduction**: Replacing the commercial distal 6-axis load cell (~0.2 kg) with embedded strain gauges or proprioceptive current-based force sensing could save notable weight.
- **Integration with Powered Feet**: The authors plan to build a QDD-powered ankle-foot module and combine it over CAN bus into a complete powered lower-limb system.

sections.heading: A Major Milestone Toward Bringing QDD Prostheses to the Clinic and Market
sections.summary: By optimizing an 18:1 gear ratio, the team built a QDD knee prosthesis matching commercial units in size and weight while delivering 145 Nm peak torque and exceptional backdrivability. This work proves that QDD architectures can become a practical mainstream approach for prosthetics.
sections.details:
Quasi-direct drive (QDD) actuators have long been labeled as high-performance yet too heavy and bulky. Through rigorous thermal and structural modeling and two-stage transmission optimization, this study condensed QDD into a 2.6 kg, 24.5 cm build height package capable of going head-to-head with commercial devices.

Benchtop tests and trials with three amputee participants confirmed high backdrivability, precise position and torque control, biomimetic kinematics and kinetics, and quiet operation. Achieving these criteria with a simple, fixed, low gear ratio—without high-impedance gearing or complex variable transmissions—is a major step forward.

Future work will expand validation to stair ascent and slope walking, while developing a modular QDD powered foot to advance lower-limb functional restoration.

sections.heading: Appendix: Motor Parameter Identification and Thermal Circuit Modeling
sections.summary: To unlock the motor's true capabilities, torque constant (0.175 Nm/A) and friction parameters were experimentally identified. In addition, an equivalent thermal circuit model mapped conduction and convection, accurately predicting the frame's heat dissipation performance.
sections.details:
### Experimental Identification of Motor Properties
Because manufacturer catalog specs are not always accurate, parameters were characterized on a dedicated test bench.
- **Torque Constant $k_{tq}$ Measurement**: Locked-rotor torque tests and back-EMF tests driven by an external motor revealed a torque constant of 0.175 Nm/A—higher than the 0.169 Nm/A nominal spec. This confirmed the motor produces target torque with less current than anticipated.
- **Friction and Damping Identification**: No-load constant speed tests and multi-speed loaded tests yielded a viscous damping coefficient $b_m = 1.306 \times 10^{-4}\text{ Nms/rad}$ and Coulomb friction $f_m = 0.062\text{ Nm}$.

### Temperature Prediction via Thermal Equivalent Circuit Modeling
Joule heating in motor windings can cause insulation failure or demagnetization. To prevent this, thermal conduction and convection were modeled as an electrical circuit network of thermal resistances ($R$) and capacitances ($C$).
- For the standalone motor, differential equations linking thermal power $Q$ to winding temperature $T_W$ were solved, and thermal parameters were fitted against infrared thermography data.
- For the chassis-mounted motor, winding-to-frame resistance $R_{WF}$, frame thermal capacity $C_F$, and frame-to-ambient resistance $R_{FA}$ were incorporated. Pairing FEA simulations with physical heat sink tests created an analytical framework predicting steady-state temperature rises within $\pm 2^\circ\text{C}$ of measured data.

takeaways: With rigorous thermal engineering and multi-objective transmission optimization, QDD actuators can match commercial powered prostheses in mass (2.6 kg) and height (24.5 cm).
A fixed 18:1 reduction allows torque tracking error below biological standard deviation—using current sensing alone without joint torque sensors—while maintaining sub-1 Nm backdrive torque.
Low gear ratios directly yield mechanical acoustic quietness (~4.8 dB peak reduction vs. a commercial high-ratio knee), substantially improving user quality of life.
Prosthetic joint ranges of motion cannot rely solely on able-bodied averages; they must accommodate deeper flexion angles required by lower-mobility users for compensatory support.
limitations: Prioritizing high peak current discharge with LiPo batteries limited continuous walking time to ~2 hours (~8,300 steps), requiring larger battery capacity and lower-power electronics for all-day commercial use.
The commercial 6-axis load cell (~0.2 kg) at the distal end imposes weight and height penalties, motivating custom strain-gauge integration or proprioceptive force estimation.
Amputee user trials were restricted to level-ground walking and sit-to-stand transitions; high-load non-level tasks like stairs and ramps remain for future testing.
